summary: Explains why it can be useful to extend IPsec with a mode that does not authenticate peers: deploying authentication credentials is often a big obstacle to using IPsec at all. It sets out the problem and applicability for Better-Than-Nothing Security. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: Setting up name tags for everybody is hard work, so many people skip locking their doors altogether. This memo argues that a lock without name tags is still better than no lock, and sets out carefully where that is true and where it is not.

questions: what is better than nothing security
subtitle: Why IPsec without peer authentication can still be better than no security, and when to use it.

tldr.problem: IPsec and IKE require the peers to authenticate, and deploying the identities and credentials to do that is often a bigger obstacle than the security itself, so many people use a higher-layer protocol instead or use nothing at all.
tldr.mechanism: BTNS relaxes the network-layer authentication requirement. Stand-Alone BTNS relies on IPsec alone, while Channel-Bound BTNS ties the security association to authentication done at a higher layer, using channel binding so that an attack on the setup is detected when the higher layer checks.
tldr.outcome: The document is a problem and applicability statement, not a specification. It sets out the six operating modes, the cases where BTNS fits, and the risks, and its central rule is that BTNS replaces no security, never stronger security.

today: RFC 5387 is an Informational document published in November 2008, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It states the problem and the applicability rather than specifying a protocol; the extension itself is in RFC 5386, and the channel binding mechanism is in RFC 5056.

sections.title: Why IPsec Is Not Widely Used
sections.content:
IPsec, made up of IKE, ESP and AH, secures IP traffic and offers protection against a wide range of threats, but authentication is required, and authentication in turn requires deploying identities and credentials, which can be an obstacle to using IPsec at all.

There are two broad approaches to authentication. Out-of-band authentication uses a trusted third party, a separate channel to the peer, or the same channel at a higher layer, and requires mechanisms and interfaces to bind the authenticated identities to the secure channels. Pre-deployed information means identities, pre-shared secrets and credentials already authenticated by trusted authorities, such as a certificate and its private key. This form often needs manual deployment and coordination between peers, and obtaining a certificate involves extra protocol and administrative steps that can take significant time and effort.

Those factors raise the work needed to use IKE with IPsec for peer authentication, so some users and applications do not protect traffic at the network layer at all, relying on higher-layer protocols such as TLS or running with no security. Higher-layer security alone may not be enough against some network-layer attacks: a transport protocol such as TCP is open to off-path attacks such as an injected TCP RST, and the Internet lacks comprehensive ingress filtering. Those attacks can affect BGP sessions between core routers, and most proposed fixes sit at the transport layer. TCP MD5 and its possible successor TCP Auth are based on authentication, while TCP-specific changes that lack authentication are at best temporary patches. The obvious answer to spoofing is end-to-end validation of the traffic, but the authentication infrastructure IPsec needs can be prohibitive, and so can the pre-shared keys TCP MD5 needs.

The core idea of BTNS is to remove the authentication requirement from IPsec instead of reducing the hurdles. It provides anonymous, unauthenticated keying so that security associations can be created with peers that do not have the needed credentials, which requires extensions to the IPsec architecture. BTNS uses a weaker notion of authenticated identity than most authentication protocols, bootstrapped from the security association itself: continuity of association. It does not mean "Bill Smith" or "owner of shared secret X2YQ", but "the entity with which I have been communicating on connection 23". It is invariant only within a single security association, not across associations, so it can only protect during the lifetime of one association.
sections.plainLanguage: IPsec insists on both ends proving who they are, and getting the paperwork and keys in place is often harder than the attack it prevents. This memo asks whether you can have the lock without the name tags, and answers: sometimes yes, as long as you know what you are giving up.

sections.title: IPsec Channels and Channel Binding
sections.content:
When IPsec security services are used by higher-layer protocols, those services must be bound to the higher-layer sessions so that they are applied consistently to the traffic involved. The result is an IPsec channel, and creating one is an instance of channel binding. A secure channel is a packet, datagram, octet stream connection or sequence of connections between two endpoints that affords cryptographic integrity and, optionally, confidentiality to the data exchanged over it. For IPsec, an IPsec channel is a packet flow associated with a higher-layer session, such as a TCP connection, where all the packets are protected by security associations such that the peer's identity is the same for the lifetime of the flow and the quality of protection is the same for all of its packets.

The endpoints of an IPsec channel are the higher-layer endpoints, which are beyond the ends of the security associations involved, so each association has to be bound to the higher-layer session and its endpoints. Failing to do that creates vulnerabilities to man-in-the-middle attacks, where what appears to be a single association is really two separate ones concatenated by an attacker acting as a traffic-forwarding proxy. Connection latching creates the channel by associating security associations with higher-layer sessions, and channel binding lets a higher-layer protocol bind its authentication to those associations. Caching the latch across sessions is needed to counter inter-session spoofing, and the channel binding authentication should be performed on each session.

Channel binding for IPsec is based on information from the association creation process that uniquely identifies a pair of associations. It can be done by adding that information to higher-layer authentication mechanisms based on one-way hashes, key exchanges or public key signatures; in all three cases the resulting higher-layer authentication resists man-in-the-middle attacks on association creation. When each IKE peer uses a public and private key pair for authentication, the pair of public keys used, one for each peer, suffices for channel binding, and strong incorporation of that information into the higher-layer authentication causes the higher-layer authentication to fail when an attacker has concatenated separate associations by acting as a proxy.
sections.plainLanguage: The layers have to agree they are talking to the same peer. A channel is the higher-layer session tied to the encrypted pipe underneath it, and channel binding is the mechanism that proves the two belong together, so that a man in the middle cannot splice two separate pipes into one that looks fine.

sections.title: What BTNS Changes in IPsec
sections.content:
The main update to IPsec is an extension to security policy that permits secure communication with unauthenticated peers. For IPsec, the first extension applies to the Peer Authorization Database, which specifies the forms of authentication allowed for each IKE peer: in addition to existing forms such as X.509 certificates and pre-shared secrets, an unauthenticated category is added in which the public key presented by the peer serves as its identity, authenticated by the peer demonstrating knowledge of the corresponding private key. The second extension adds a flag to each Security Policy Database entry to say whether the absence of authentication is acceptable for that entry. The changes needed to enable channel binding between IPsec and higher layers are more complex, requiring APIs and interactions between IPsec and the higher-layer protocols, and the document assumes such provisions will be developed without describing them.

The changes affect IPsec policy mainly; other parts of the IPsec and IKE specifications are unchanged, and BTNS does not require a separate IPsec implementation, because it can be integrated with any implementation. Its scope applies only to the associations matching policies that explicitly enable BTNS modes and whose security policy entries allow it. Other policy entries and non-BTNS associations are unaffected. In principle, removing the requirement that all associations be authenticated means BTNS can establish secure connections much like fully authenticated IKE, but BTNS cannot verify or authenticate the peer identities.

The effect on the IPsec security services is as follows. Access control is extended to allow unauthenticated connections, integrated with the PAD and SPD without affecting entries that do not use the extensions; for Channel-Bound BTNS, the authentication that applies to the association is performed at a higher layer, linking higher-layer access control policy to IPsec's network-layer mechanisms. Data origin authentication is weakened by Stand-Alone BTNS to continuity of association, the assurance that traffic on an association continues to come from the same unauthenticated source, while Channel-Bound BTNS relies on higher-layer authentication to provide it. The remaining services, connectionless integrity, anti-replay protection, confidentiality and limited traffic flow confidentiality, can be used to establish connections with rogue peers, because authentication is not required, but once a secure connection is established the communication is protected in the same way as with conventional IPsec.
sections.plainLanguage: The change to IPsec itself is small: a new kind of entry saying "the peer's key is its name" and a flag on each policy entry saying "an unauthenticated peer is fine here". Everything else, encryption, integrity and replay protection, works exactly as before once the connection is up.

sections.title: The Six Operating Modes
sections.content:
There are two classes of scenario in which BTNS can be used to apply IPsec services without network-layer authentication. The first protects traffic for a higher-layer protocol that does not use authentication: the protection is better than nothing because once an unauthenticated association is created without a man in the middle, its security services resist later man-in-the-middle attacks, even though the absence of authentication allows the creation itself to be subverted. This is Stand-Alone BTNS, or SAB, because it relies on nothing outside IPsec. The second protects traffic generated by a higher-layer protocol that does use authentication: the protection relies on the strength of that authentication and on the channel binding of it to the BTNS associations, and may be comparable to network-layer IKE authentication when the higher-layer protocol uses strong authentication and strong channel binding. This is Channel-Bound BTNS, or CBB, when the combination is enough to detect a man-in-the-middle attack on the creation of the association.

It is possible to combine IKE authentication for one end of a pair with the absence of network-layer authentication for the other, giving asymmetric modes. Combining the two ways of using BTNS with the possibility of symmetric or asymmetric operation gives six modes. AUTH is the ordinary case, where both parties provide and authenticate conventional IKE-supported identities. Symmetric SAB is where neither party authenticates with a conventional IKE-supported identity, and asymmetric SAB is where one party does and the other does not. CB-AUTH uses channel binding with both parties authenticating conventionally. Symmetric CBB is where neither party authenticates conventionally but channel binding ties the associations to higher-layer authentication, and asymmetric CBB is asymmetric SAB with channel binding.

Three security mechanisms are involved in channel-bound BTNS: BTNS and IPsec at the network layer, higher-layer authentication, and the connection latching plus channel binding that ties the higher-layer credentials to the secure IPsec channel. Authentication at both the network and higher layers can be bidirectional or unidirectional, but when channel binding is used it must be applied at both ends to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks, and existing channel binding mechanisms mandate the exchange and verification of the binding values at both ends. When SAB or CBB is used without being qualified as symmetric or asymmetric, the symmetric mode is the intended default.
sections.plainLanguage: Six combinations are possible, depending on whether each end proves its identity and whether the higher layer is tied to the encrypted pipe. The names are short for that: AUTH, symmetric and asymmetric SAB, and symmetric and asymmetric CBB. Unqualified, the symmetric form is meant.

sections.title: When BTNS Fits
sections.content:
BTNS is intended for services open to the public but where protected associations are wanted, and for services that can be authenticated at higher layers. It can also give some protection to private services where the alternative is no protection at all. It uses the IPsec suite, so it should not be used where IPsec and IKE are unsuitable: both cost computation, and IKE costs round-trip latency in setting up associations, which may be undesirable with limited computing resources or high latency.

The benefits are that associations are protected once established, because the network and transport layers are protected without network-layer authentication; BTNS can be deployed with no pre-deployed authentication material and can protect all transport protocols with one mechanism; simple transport-layer packet attacks are rejected because the malicious packets are not part of an association, so an attacker has to establish an unauthenticated association and a transport connection, which takes as much work as a real participant, raising the effort needed for a denial-of-service attack to that of emulating a flash crowd.

The vulnerabilities follow from the same design. Because every association need not be authenticated, a host connecting to a BTNS host is vulnerable to communicating with a masquerader throughout the association, or until higher layers add authentication, so passwords sent to a masquerading peer could be disclosed. This is a deliberate trade-off, and the reverse also holds: BTNS can secure connections to hosts that cannot authenticate at the network layer, so the network and transport layers are better protected than higher-layer authentication alone could achieve. Without network-layer authentication information, other means must provide access control for local resources: traffic selectors on the BTNS policy entries can limit which interfaces, address ranges and port ranges may reach BTNS-enabled services, and rate limiting can restrict resource use. For SAB these protections have to hold for the whole association, while for CBB they are needed only until the higher layer supplies the missing authentication.

Stand-Alone BTNS suits applications that cannot use IKE-compatible credentials and do not use higher-layer authentication, and also cases where the identities of either party do not matter or are deliberately omitted but IPsec services are wanted. It is particularly applicable to long-lived connections where assurance that the entity at the other end has not changed is a good enough substitute for authentication: large file transfers that should not be cut short by an attack on the transport connection, such as a false TCP RST, benefit from it even when the particular endpoint identities are unimportant. Open services such as web servers and peer-to-peer networks could use symmetric SAB, as could voice-over-IP calls between peers, and any transport protocol whose endpoints deploy no authentication, which includes the TCP connections between core routers running BGP. Symmetric SAB can also be an intermediate step towards the channel-bound form.

Asymmetric SAB lets a party without network-layer credentials establish associations with a party that has them, which suits open services such as commercial web servers: the server is typically authenticated by a widely known authority, as with TLS, while the clients need not be. Using IPsec and TLS on the same connection duplicates security services at different layers, and the document argues that duplication is necessary, because TLS cannot stop a spoofed TCP RST, which TCP processes rather than passing to TLS.

Channel-Bound BTNS lets hosts without network-layer credentials bind their BTNS associations cryptographically to authentication at higher layers. It suits applications that authenticate at a higher layer but also want network-layer security, and it lets IPsec be used with authentication mechanisms IKE does not support, freeing higher-layer applications from duplicating services IPsec already provides. Symmetric CBB combines channel binding with symmetric SAB and asymmetric CBB with asymmetric SAB. Because higher-layer authentication can itself be one-way or two-way, asymmetric CBB can complement one-way higher-layer authentication by providing one-way authentication of the opposite direction at the network layer, which achieves mutual authentication at separate layers; remote file system protocols such as iSCSI and NFS fit this category and can benefit from channel binding, including protection against man-in-the-middle attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: BTNS fits where the alternative is no protection: open services, long file transfers that should not be cut off, and applications that authenticate further up the stack. It does not fit where you genuinely need to know who is on the other end, and it is no substitute for real authentication.

sections.title: The Risks
sections.content:
BTNS is intended to protect sessions from on-path attacks, from man-in-the-middle attacks after key exchange and from off-path attacks. It protects the contents of a session once established, but not the establishment itself, which forces the attacker to target the setup rather than wait for a more convenient time, and that is of particular value for long-lived sessions. It is not intended to protect the key exchange, which leaves an opening for a man-in-the-middle or a well-timed attack, and Stand-Alone BTNS does not protect an endpoint from nodes masquerading as legitimate clients of a higher-layer service, while Channel-Bound BTNS can, though only later, when the higher-layer authentication fails. BTNS is also not intended to protect against denial-of-service attacks that overload a CPU doing authentication, nor against configuration mistakes, and those assumptions hold for IPsec as well.

On the man-in-the-middle and masquerader side, the difference from ordinary IPsec is when the attack is found. With regular IPsec and IKE, an attacker concatenating two associations causes an IKE authentication failure straight away. With channel-bound BTNS, IKE succeeds because it is unauthenticated, the associations are set up, and the attacker is discovered only when the higher-layer authentication fails, which raises two concerns: possible exposure of sensitive authentication information, and resource consumption before the attack is detected. Whether information is exposed depends on the higher-layer protocol. If the higher-layer authentication exchanges sensitive material that is directly useful or can be attacked offline, the attacker gains it even though the attack is detected, so BTNS must not be used with higher-layer protocols that may expose sensitive information during the exchange: a Kerberos service ticket exchange would leak little beyond the target's principal name, but a Kerberos authentication exchange using timestamp pre-authentication would leak material that can be attacked offline, and that should not be used with BTNS even with channel binding.

On denial of service, more traffic needs cryptographic operations, which raises the computation required in implementations that protect or verify traffic, and that raises the vulnerability to overloading, whether from a flash crowd or an attack; this is an issue for all cryptographically protected systems. The extra cost also raises the effort needed for attacks, but consumes more resources to detect them and reject spoofed traffic, so proper limits and access controls should be set up for all BTNS associations, channel-bound associations may be granted increased resource access after the higher-layer authentications succeed, and special care is needed to avoid excessive resource use before authentication is established.

Using SAB means the service is offered for open access, since no network-layer authentication is performed, so it should not be used with services not intended to be openly available. ICMP attacks are not considered, because BTNS does not change the existing IPsec guidelines on ICMP handling; it focuses on the authentication part of establishing associations and does not alter the traffic processing model or protection boundary.

BTNS also allows a kind of "Leap of Faith" behaviour, like SSH, which may accept a peer's public key without authenticating it and cache it for later. There are differences: SSH requires proper warnings and options in applications to reject unauthenticated credentials, while BTNS accepts them automatically when they match the policy entries; SSH requires the credential to be cached and reused, while BTNS caching is allowed but pointless, because any new unauthenticated credential allowed by the policy is accepted automatically anyway. Adding Leap of Faith to BTNS would need warnings, a mechanism for user acceptance or rejection, and a way to deal with the absence of identities, and it would run into trouble with NATs, which can make several sources look like one, multihoming, which can make one source look like several, and with mobility and address ownership changes.

On rekeying, every association has a limited lifetime and must be rekeyed or terminated, and rekeying gives an on-path attacker a small window to hijack the new association by spoofing the victim. BTNS, and particularly SAB, simplify the attack by removing the need for the attacker to authenticate as the victim, while CBB can detect such attacks by noticing the change in the secure channel properties. The underlying cause is the lack of inter-session binding or latching of the IKE associations with the peers' credentials, and connection latching with channel binding would supply that binding, but it requires the higher-layer protocols to verify that identities and authentication are consistent across the two associations. Finally, BTNS does not address configuration errors that increase vulnerability, which is already possible with bypass policy entries, but entries that allow BTNS must be explicitly flagged and so can be kept separate from entries that create associations with stronger security.
sections.plainLanguage: The lock works once the door is shut, but not while it is being fitted. Somebody can be in the room while the two sides agree a key, and with the standalone form nobody ever checks who is there. The memo is firm that this is only ever a substitute for no lock at all.
